section_title: What can Egypt’s idols, river and advisers do when judgment comes?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 This is the burden against Egypt: Behold, the LORD rides on a swift cloud; He is coming to Egypt. The idols of Egypt will tremble before Him, and the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them. 2 “So I will incite Egyptian against Egyptian; brother will fight against brother, neighbor against neighbor, city against city, and kingdom against kingdom. 3 Then the spirit of the Egyptians will be emptied out from among them, and I will frustrate their plans, so that they will resort to idols and spirits of the dead, to mediums and spiritists. 4 I will deliver the Egyptians into the hands of a harsh master, and a fierce king will rule over them,” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts.

5 The waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty. 6 The canals will stink; the streams of Egypt will trickle and dry up; the reeds and rushes will wither. 7 The bulrushes by the Nile, by the mouth of the river, and all the fields sown along the Nile, will wither, blow away, and be no more. 8 Then the fishermen will mourn, all who cast a hook into the Nile will lament, and those who spread nets on the waters will pine away. 9 The workers in flax will be dismayed, and the weavers of fine linen will turn pale. 10 The workers in cloth will be dejected, and all the hired workers will be sick at heart.

11 The princes of Zoan are mere fools; Pharaoh’s wise counselors give senseless advice. How can you say to Pharaoh, “I am one of the wise, a son of eastern kings”? 12 Where are your wise men now? Let them tell you and reveal what the LORD of Hosts has planned against Egypt. 13 The princes of Zoan have become fools; the princes of Memphis are deceived. The cornerstones of her tribes have led Egypt astray. 14 The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion. Egypt has been led astray in all she does, as a drunkard staggers through his own vomit. 15 There is nothing Egypt can do— head or tail, palm or reed.

context_lines: The message against Egypt opens with the Lord riding on a swift cloud. Its idols tremble, and the people lose heart. The Lord announces conflict within the country, failed plans, resort to forbidden spiritual counsel, and rule by a harsh master.

The drying of the Nile reaches through the fields and working life of the land. Fishermen mourn, plants wither, and those who work in flax and cloth lose their livelihood. The passage makes the disruption visible through the people and occupations affected by it.

The warning then confronts Pharaoh’s counselors. Their claims to wisdom cannot reveal what the Lord has planned, and those who should guide Egypt instead lead it astray. Confusion is pictured as a drunkard staggering through his own vomit.

The closing line includes head and tail, palm and reed: Egypt is helpless across its ranks. The chapter has exposed the failure of its religious, material and political sources of confidence before turning to a different future in the following verses.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/19.htm) and [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/19.htm) read the civil conflict, harsh rule and failed counsel as the Lord’s judgment on Egypt’s false security. Both emphasize that celebrated human wisdom cannot protect a people whose plans stand against Him.

There is less agreement on the ruler in verse 4. Wesley identifies Psammetichus; [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/19.htm) discusses that identification alongside other proposed rulers. The text itself leaves the harsh master unnamed, so the warning can be explained without treating one historical identification as certain.

Wesley and Gill also discuss whether the river language is a picture of lost power and trade or a description of the Nile’s waters failing. Both give weight to the physical effects described in the following verses.
